In the Court of Appeal of Alberta

Citation: Christie v. Greiger, 1986 ABCA
206

Date:
19861028

Docket:
18543

Registry:
Edmonton

Between:

Douglas Christie

Plaintiff

(Respondent)

- and -

John Geiger and the Edmonton Sun, a Division of

the Toronto Sun Publishing Corporation

Defendants

(Appellants)

The Court:

The Honourable Mr. Justice McClung

The Honourable Mr. Justice Belzil

The Honourable Mr. Justice Irving

Reasons for Judgment of The Honourable Mr.
Justice McClung

Concurred in by The Honourable Mr. Justice
Irving

Dissenting Reasons of The Honourable Mr.
Justice Belzil

APPEAL FROM THE JUDGMENT OF THE HONOURABLE
MR. JUSTICE R.P. FOISY DATED DECEMBER 4, 1984

COUNSEL:

Barry Zalmanowitz, Esq., for the Appellants

DUNCAN L. McKillop, Esq., for the Respondent

REASONS FOR
JUDGMENT OF

THE HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE McCLUNG

[
1
]

The defendants appeal an award of damages for
defamatory libel recovered in the Court of Queen’s Bench.

Origins

[
2
]

The plaintiff is a lawyer and freedom of speech
activist carrying on the bulk of his legal practice in British Columbia. In the
early 1980s he sought and gained political attention throughout the west by his
road show promotion of Western Separatism. A series of public forums were held.
He brought this action upon the July 1981 publication of an “editorial”
criticism written by the appellant Geiger which was published by the appellant
The Edmonton Sun, a newspaper circulated in Edmonton and northern Alberta. The
article included:

“So Doug Christie and his group of
misfits known collectively as Western Canada Concept (WCC) plan to run a
candidate in Olds-Didsbury once a provincial by-election is called. There could
not be better news for Canadians who want to rid themselves of this collection
of throwbacks.

For close to a year we have seen publications
like Alberta Report give these losers some credibility: they have actually
taken seriously the right-wing rantings of WCC’s Christie and West-Fed’s Elmer
Knutson. They made it appear that Western separatism was fairly
wide-spread--when in reality it is just an Alberta version of the Ku Klux Klan.

If Doug and his WCC slugs attract any
votes at all in Olds-Didsbury it will be from the lunatic fringe, and perhaps a
couple of farmers who have spent too many summer days in the hot Alberta sun.
Separation in Alberta was never a mass movement. It just made for good
conversation at business luncheons.”

[
3
]

While the trial examined several complaints
arising from the publication, the record reveals that the plaintiff’s real
concern fastened upon the statement:

“… when in reality it is just an Alberta version of the Ku Klux Klan”.

The trial judge, Foisy
J., held that the statement injured Christie in the sense that when it was
fairly read the allusion linked him with the virulent racial and anti-Roman
Catholic pursuits of the Ku Klux Klan. The learned trial judge found, and the
evidence supports his conclusion, that the reach of the offending reference
included the plaintiff, who by 1981 was the leader of the Western Canada
Concept. It was a society formed by him to promote Western Canadian
independence by constitutional means. Damages were awarded.

[
4
]

Mr. Geiger, the author, intended to convey a
peremptory indictment of western independence generally. Those politics were,
of course, a fair reportive and editorial target. But to intensify his
rejection of Christie and his cause, he invoked, seemingly off-the-wall, the
searing but incongruous Ku Klux Klan reference. Foisy J. accepted the
plaintiff’s evidence that his personal ideals and those he advanced politically
were free from racial incentive. He resolved the question as follows:

“Initially it is clear that there are actually several statements of
fact. The article refers to Western separation as ‘Just an Alberta version of
the Ku Klux Klan’. This statement expresses the fact of some association
between Western separatists, a class in which the Plaintiff is clearly
identified, and the racist organization the Ku Klux Klan.

All of the evidence led by the parties demonstrates exactly the
opposite. There was no association or similarity in activities or beliefs of
the Plaintiff or W.C.C. and the Ku Klux Klan. Indeed, expert evidence described
the Ku Klux Klan as preaching hatred of Roman Catholics and Blacks. The
Plaintiff, Christie, is a practicing Roman Catholic. The declared policies of
the W.C.C. and its forerunner, the Committee for Western Independence,
consistently discuss economic and political issues without any racial, ethnic
or prejudicial overtones. Evidence led of the Plaintiff. Christie’s personal
beliefs, conduct and actions would lead one to the conclusion that he is a very
sincere individual who clearly demonstrated on numerous occasions that he would
not tolerate prejudicial or racial comments to be made at W.C.C. meetings. He
demonstrated admirable tolerance of dissenting and often unfair and disruptive
comments made at the meetings of the W.C.C. The Defendants have failed to show
the allegation of fact to be accurate.”

[
5
]

These positive findings are inseparable from the
evidence that was offered at the trial. On appeal, Mr. Zalmanowitz referred to
anti-francophone invective voiced at some of the rumbustious W.C.C. meetings.
But the hostile sentiment was not brought home to the plaintiff who, the trial
judge found, had condemned it.

[
6
]

The pleaded defence of truth must fail.

Fair Comment

[
7
]

Additional argument was taken in an attempt to
shelter the offending words as fair comment as opposed to fact. The submission
flows from the plaintiff’s obvious election to place himself under the public
spotlight. In specifics it was urged that the trial judge did not delineate
between comment and fact. While the reserved reasons for judgment of the trial
judge are not chaptered between mere comment on fact, fact alone and the legal
considerations arising from each, the reasons as a whole reveal that the
critical distinctions between fact and comment could not have been lost to the
court. Some evidence of this is found in the judgment’s extended citation of
the core principles relating to the pleaded defences of truth and fair comment
upon which the case turned. For example:

“Fair comment must be based on fact
…

A comment is not protected if it appears to be an allegation of
fact. For the defence to hold, the ordinary unprejudiced reader must take the
remarks to be a comment based on fact. Thus if the ‘sting of the words
complained of do not appear to be comment at all the defence will fail
…”

Linden
. Canadian Tort Law, 8th Ed., pp. 711-712. (Emphasis that of Foisy
J.)

“For the defence to be available it must be indicated with reasonable
clarity, by the words themselves, taking them in their context and the
circumstances in which they were published, that they purport to be comment and
not statements of fact
…

Comment cannot be fair if based on facts which are distorted or
invented
.”

Fleming
. The Law of Torts, 5th Ed., pp. 574-575. (Emphasis that of Foisy
J.)

[
8
]

In addition, the trial judge drew at length from
the current edition of
Gatley on Libel and Slander
.

[
9
]

The appellants’ submission is further weakened
by the introductory wording that was chosen by the author. The words “… in
reality …” promise the reader fact, not abstraction.

[
10
]

We are unable to conclude that the judgment
confuses what were allegations of fact in the article as opposed to comment and
the legal immunities available to each. Even if it were mere comment, malice
not being an issue, the offending reference fails the test of privilege reduced
by Dickson J. (as he then was), while dissenting under other considerations, in

Cherneskey v. Armadale Publishers
1978 CanLII 20 (SCC)
, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 1067. to:

“… if a defendant raises the defence of
fair comment, he has the burden of establishing that the facts on which it is
based are true and that it is
objectively
fair; …”

[
11
]

Under the test so stated, we are obliged to
agree with Foisy J. that the racial allusion in the offending publication was
neither privileged comment nor objectively fair.

Canadian Charter
of Rights and Freedoms

[
12
]

Despite its publication in July, 1981, the
appellants urge that the offending article is protected by the freedoms
enumerated in
s. 2(b)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
,
proclaimed
on April 17, 1982. Retrospective application of freedom of expression under

s.2
(b) escorts the appellants’ submission that the defence of fair comment
obliges a public figure who elects to sue in defamation to shoulder heavy
evidentiary burdens. Mr. Zalmanowitz invites us to declare that reasonable
limitations curtailing freedom of expression, could not, under the
Charter,
exceed
the vicissitudes of proof laid down in
New York Times v. Sullivan
(1964)
376 U.S. 254. The burden of proof that he proposes is one of proof of actual
malice motivating the publication, to be established by knowledge of its
falsity or reckless disregard of its truth. But the safe anchorage of New
York
Times v. Sullivan
is not available to these appellants simply because of
the date of the publication. Freedom of expression as enumerated in the
Charter
of Rights and Freedoms
has no application in this case if only on the issue
of retrospectivity. That was the reasoned conclusion of Foisy, J. a result
later confirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Fraser v. Public Service
Staff Relations Board.
1985 CanLII 14 (SCC)
, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 455.

[
13
]

Whether the standards of proof of New
York
Times v. Sullivan
take support from the
Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms

will be decided in a timely case. For the purposes of this case we
simply reject the argument, pressed in New
York Times
v. Sullivan,
that
defamation is inherent in media discussion of public affairs and personages.

Damages

[
14
]

Damages are an appeal issue. Although the
plaintiff was unable to prove economic loss, the trial judge measured his
damage at $30,000.00. However, the case at trial was regarded by Foisy, J. as
an
ad hominem
attack upon the plaintiff and his personal beliefs. As
such, it perpetuated the offending article.

[
15
]

Account must be taken of reaffimation of the
libel during the trial, the wide publication established in the evidence and
the range of awards in other cases, such as
Cherneskey
v. Armadale
Publishers
, supra,
dealing with unsupportable and unprotected accusations
of racism laid against public figures. Under these considerations we will not
revise the sum awarded.

[
16
]

We view the judgment as supported by the
evidence and the authorities and would dismiss the appeal with costs.

DATED at EDMONTON, Alberta

this 28th Day of October,

A.D. 1986.

REASONS FOR
JUDGMENT OF

THE HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE BELZIL

[
17
]

This is an appeal from a judgment for
defamation. The issue is whether the learned trial judge erred in ruling that
the defence of fair comment was not available.

[
18
]

The action arises out of an article written by
the appellant Geiger, a university student and free-lance columnist, and
published in the Edmonton Sun on July 14, 1981. The Edmonton Sun is a division
of The Toronto Sun Publishing Corporation.

[
19
]

The respondent is a member of the bars of
British Columbia. Alberta and the Yukon Territory and the founder of a
political party, Western Canada Concept, (hereafter referred to as W.C.C.)
whose primary political objective was the separation of the four Western
provinces from the rest of Canada. As leader of the party, the respondent
advocated his separatist views extensively in Alberta and other parts of
Western Canada, through political meetings and the resulting inevitable
coverage in the news media.

[
20
]

The same historical period saw the formation and
parallel rise of a second group advocating the separation of Western Canada,
under the leadership of one, Elmer Knutson. This group became known as
West-Fed. It too advanced its views through meetings and literature and
received extensive publicity through the media. It did not, like W.C.C. seek
status as a registered political party but advocated the achievement of its
objective by a unilateral declaration of withdrawal from the Canadian confederation.

[
21
]

Publication of the article which is the subject
matter of this lawsuit was prompted by the calling of a provincial by-election
in the constituency of Olds-Didsbury and the announcement by the W.C.C. that it
would field a candidate for it. The article appeared in the Edmonton Sun issue
of July 14, 1981, entitled in large type “Separating the goats and sheep” under
the name and photograph of the appellant Geiger. While defamation is alleged in
the three opening paragraphs only, which are highlighted, these are better
understood in the context of the entire article:

“So Doug Christie and his group of misfits known collectively as
Western Canada
Concept (WCC) plan to
run a candidate in Olds-Didsbury once a provincial by-election is called. There
could not be better news for Canadians who want to rid themselves of this
collection of throwbacks.

For close to a year we have seen publications like Alberta Report
give these losers some credibility: they have actually taken seriously the
right-wing rantings of WCC’s Christie and West-Fed’s Elmer Knutson. They made
it appear that Western separatism was fairly wide-spread - when in reality it
is just an Alberta version of the Ku Klux Klan.

If Doug and his WCC slugs attract any votes at all in Olds-Didsbury
it will be from the lunatic fringe, and perhaps a couple of farmers who have
spent too many summer days in the hot Alberta sun. Separatism in Alberta was
never a mass movement. It just made for good conversation at business
luncheons.

If separatism were a major movement in the West, as Alberta Report
seems to suggest, then why has Elmer Knutson not tried to register West-Fed as
a political party to test his support. In the past Elmer has seemed desperate
for political office, he even went so far as to challenge a respected member of
Parliament Doug Roche for his Conservative candidacy. It seems obvious that
Elmer has not put his program to the electorate because he knows he probably
wouldn’t get twenty votes.

Two weeks ago at the legislative grounds more Albertans turned out
to celebrate Canada Day than have probably ever attended a separatist meeting.
These Canadians were there despite the fact that the premier was not, despite
the fact that the lieutenant-governor was not, and despite the fact that no
representative of the provincial cabinet was there. They were there because
Albertans believe in Canada and a united future. Despite the best efforts of a
few misfits, Canada is as strong today as it has ever been, and on that bright,
sunny July First the future of Canada looked promising indeed.

The participation of Western Canada Concept in the Olds-Didbury
by-election and in the next provincial election will be a welcome addition. But
despite Doug’s and Elmer’s best efforts separatists appear to most Albertans to
be little more than a splinter group of the Rhino party.

I wonder if Elmer was out watching the fireworks on Canada Day, or
whether he and Doug spent the day at home sulking.”

[
22
]

Without singling out the particular words in the
first three paragraphs which he found to be defamatory of the plaintiff, the
learned trial judge said:

“I apply the objective test of the
ordinary reasonable man. I find as a fact that these words clearly refer to the
Plaintiff, using the common ordinary meaning of the words they attribute
demeaning and derogatory conduct, condition and abilities to the Plaintiff. In
addition, using the ordinary meaning of the words they associate the Plaintiff
with the racist organization the Ku Klux Klan.”

[
23
]

From this I conclude that the “sting” words which
the learned trial judge found capable of being defamatory are in the last
sentence of the second paragraph, namely:

“They made it appear that Western
separatism was fairly wide-spread - when in reality it is just an Alberta
version of the Ku Klux Klan.”

[
24
]

In his statement of claim, the plaintiff
ascribed the following meaning to the words which the learned trial judge found
to be defamatory:

“8. The said words in their material and
ordinary meaning meant, were understood to mean and were intended by the Defendants
to mean that the party which the Plaintiff was leader of and founded by the
Plaintiff was ‘in reality just an Alberta version of the Ku Klux Klan.’

9. Further or in the alternative the
words meant and were intended to and understood to mean

(A) The
Plaintiff ascribed to or was a supporter of the racist and white supremacist
theories of a secret American Society known as the Ku Klux Klan

….

(D) The
Plaintiff alleges the Ku Klux Klan is a racist group of strange practice
involving practices totally unkown to the Plaintiff but widely reported in the
sensationalist press.”

[
25
]

I agree with the learned trial judge that these
words in the meaning assigned to them by the learned trial judge could
associate the respondent with the racist organization the Ku Klux Klan, and
that they are capable of being defamatory. In
Cherneskey v. Armadale
Publishers Ltd.

(1978)
1978 CanLII 20 (SCC)
, 90 D.L.R. (3d) 321 (S.C.C.) the Supreme Court of
Canada held that an allegation of racism was capable of being defamatory.

[
26
]

The next determination which the learned trial
judge then had to make was whether the impugned statement was a comment on fact
or a statement of fact.

[
27
]

The distinction between comment on facts and
statement of facts is not always apparent, but is one which must absolutely be
made in defamation actions. It is at the very root of the common law’s
guarantee of freedom of opinion and expression, including freedom of the press,
essential to a truly democratic society. In determining whether words are
capable of being defamatory, the distinction is one without a difference, but
in considering the defence of fair comment the distinction becomes crucial. If
the impugned statement is one of fact, made without legal justification, the
action falls or stands with the truth of the statement and the defence of fair
comment does not arise. But if the statement is opinion, the defence of fair
comment is available providing the remaining criteria are met.

[
28
]

On the necessity and reason for distinguishing
between fact and comment, Martland J. in
Cherneskey

adopted the
following passage from
Salmond on Torts
:

“A fair comment on a matter which is of public interest or is
submitted to public criticism is not actionable. This right is one of the
aspects of the fundamental principle of freedom of expression, and the courts
are zealous to preserve it unimpaired. It must not be whittled down by legal
refinements. The jury are the guardians of the freedom of public comment as
well as of private character. It is only on the strongest grounds that a court
will set aside a verdict for a defendant when fair comment is pleaded.

Comment or criticism must be carefully distinguished from a
statement of fact. The former is not actionable if it relates to a matter which
is of public interest; the latter is actionable, even though the facts so
stated would, if true, have possessed the greatest public interest and
importance. Comment or criticism is essentially a statement of opinion as to
the estimate to be formed of a man’s writings or actions. Being therefore a
mere matter of opinion, and so incapable of definite proof, he who expresses it
is not called upon by the law to justify it as being true, but is allowed to
express it, even though others disagree with it, provided that it is honest.”

[
29
]

While he did not specifically say so, it must be
assumed that the learned trial judge considered the impugned statement to be
comment on fact and not a statement of fact because he went on to consider at
length the defence of fair comment. This defence would not even arise and he
would not have considered it at all had he found the statement to be one of
fact.

[
30
]

That it was comment on fact is consistent with
the meaning pleaded in the statement of claim “that the plaintiff ascribed to
or was supportive of the racist and white supremacist
theories
” of the
Ku Klux Klan. The reference to the Ku Klux Klan is metaphor, made for
comparison purposes, an expression of opinion, the product of the mind of the
person making it.

[
31
]

While quoting extensively from Gatley it is
apparent, with all respect, that the trial judge misunderstood the defence of
fair comment and applied the wrong test.

[
32
]

The learned trial judge fell into the very error
warned against by Lord Diplock in his charge to the jury in
Silkin v.
Beaverbrook Newspapers Ltd. infra.
Excerpts from that charge were approved
by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Cherneskey
supra.
The first excerpt
was approved by Martland, J., at p. 325:

“A clear statement of the nature of the defence of fair comment is
found in the summing up to the jury of Diplock, J. (as he then was), in the
case of
Silkin v. Beaverbrook Newspapers Ltd.,
(1958) 1 W.L.R. 743 at
p.747
.
[1958] 2 All E.R. 516
:

I have been referring, and counsel in their speeches to you have
been referring, to fair comment, because that is the technical name which is
given to this defence, or, as I should prefer to say, which is given to the
right of every citizen to comment on matters of public interest.
But the
expression ‘fair comment’ is a little misleading. It may give you the
impression that you, the jury, have to decide
whether you agree with the
comment, whether you think it is fair. If that were the question you had to
decide, you realize that the limits of freedom which the law allows would be
greatly curtailed.
People are entitled to hold and to express freely on
matters of public interest strong views, views which some of you, or indeed all
of you, may think are exaggerated, obstinate or prejudiced, provided - and this
is the important thing - that they are views which they honestly hold. The
basis of our public life is that the crank, the enthusiast, may say what he
honestly thinks just as much as the reasonable man or woman who sits on a jury
,
and it would be a sad day for freedom of speech in this country if a
jury
were to apply the test of whether it agrees with the comment instead of
applying the true test: was this an opinion, however exaggerated, obstinate or
prejudiced, which was honestly held by the writer
?” (emphasis mine)

[
33
]

The second excerpt from Lord Diplock’s charge is
that adopted by Dickson, J. (as he then was), (dissenting on other grounds).

“Could a fair-minded man, holding a
strong view, holding perhaps an obstinate view, holding perhaps a prejudiced
view - could a fair-minded man have been capable of writing this? That is a
totally different question from the question: Do you agree with what he said?

So in considering this case, members of the jury,
do not apply
the test of whether you agree with it
. If juries did that, freedom of
speech, the right of the crank to say what he likes, would go.
Would a
fair-minded man holding strong views, obstinate views, prejudiced views, have
been capable of making this comment
. If the answer to that is yes, then
your verdict in this case should be a verdict for the defendants. Such a
verdict does not mean that you agree with the comment. All it means if that you
think that a man might honestly hold those views on those facts.” (emphasis
mine)

[
34
]

The learned trial judge rejected the defence of
fair comment for the very reason that he found it to be unfair and did not
agree with it. He failed to consider or apply the test in Lord Diplock’s charge
as approved by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Cherneskey
.
He seemed to
have treated the impugned statement which he had first considered to be comment
as an allegation of fact to be proven accurate to sustain the defence of fair
comment. In dealing with the defence of fair comment he said:

“The article refers to Western separation
as ‘just an Alberta version of the Ku Klux Klan’. This statement expresses the
fact of some association between Western separatists, a class in which the
Plaintiff is clearly identified, and the racist organization the Ku Klux Klan.

All of the evidence led by the parties demonstrates exactly the
opposite. There was no association or
similarity in activities or beliefs

of the Plaintiff or W.C.C. and the Ku Klux Klan. Indeed, expert evidence
described the Ku Klux Klan as preaching hatred of Roman Catholics and Blacks.
The Plaintiff, Christie, is a practicing Roman Catholic. The declared policies
of the W.C.C. and its forerunner, the Committee for Western Independence,
consistently discuss economic and political issues without any racial, ethnic
or prejudicial overtones. Evidence led of the Plaintiff, Christie’s
personal
beliefs, conduct and actions
would lead one to the conclusion that he is a
very sincere individual who clearly demonstrated on numerous occasions that he
would not tolerate prejudicial or racial comments to be made at W.C.C.
meetings. He demonstrated admirable tolerance of dissenting and often unfair
and disruptive comments made at the meetings of the W.C.C. The Defendants have
failed to show the allegation of fact to be accurate.” (emphasis mine)

[
35
]

The next succeeding paragraph of his reasons
makes it even more apparent that the learned trial judge did not appreciate the
difference between fact and comment on fact. In dealing with the part of the
impugned statement forecasting (wrongly as it turned out) the results of the
forthcoming by-election in Olds-Didsbury, even though he had not found that
part of the statement to be capable of being defamatory, he said:

“Further, another statement of fact is that the only persons who
would vote for the W.C.C. in Olds-Didsbury were ‘the lunatic fringe, and
perhaps a couple of farmers who have spent too many summer days in the hot Alberta sun.’ Yet the W.C.C. easily won
that by-election. In the general Provincial election held shortly thereafter
the W.C.C. gained 12% of the popular vote. Mr. Geiger in cross-examination held
to his statement that these people must be part of the ‘lunatic fringe’. The
evidence was clear, that many respected individuals supported the W.C.C. and
were clearly not part of any ‘lunatic fringe’.

An expert called to prove the truth of this fact had considerable
difficulty not finding the N.D.P. part of such a ‘fringe’ group with
historically 9-10% of the popular vote in Federal elections and 15-18% of the
popular vote in Provincial elections. Ideology may be why Mr. Geiger finds
conservatives generally to be ‘throwbacks’ but that ungenerous belief does not
make it into the truth.”

[
36
]

By its very nature a forecast of future events
is not capable of being a statement of fact.

[
37
]

In the face of these fundamental errors the
judgment cannot be sustained.

[
38
]

What remains to be considered is whether this
court can determine whether the defence of fair comment has been made out on
the evidence, or whether a new trial must be directed. In my view there is
sufficient uncontradicted evidence to establish the defence. While the learned
trial judge rejected some of the opinions of the expert Pratt, he did not
question the facts observed by Pratt at a meeting which he attended. There is
no issue of credibility on the facts.

[
39
]

In
Cherneskey

(
supra
) Dickson J.,
(dissenting on other grounds) adopted the following main principles of the
defence of fair comment from the textbook of
Duncan and Neill on Defamation

(1978):

“(a)   the comment must be on a matter of public interest;

(b)    the comment must be based on fact;

(c)    the comment, though it can include inferences of fact, must
be recognisable as comment;

(d)    the comment must satisfy the following objective test: could
any man honestly express that opinion on the proved facts?;

(e)    even though the comment satisfies the objective test the
defence can be defeated if the plaintiff proves that the defendant was actuated
by express malice.”

[
40
]

Are the five conditions met in this case?

[
41
]

Since questions a) c) and e) can readily be
answered on the evidence, I will dispose of these first, leaving for final
consideration the more difficult question posed in condition (b) and condition
(d) which is closely related to it.

[
42
]

That the matters being commented on were matters
of public interest is self evident. The learned trial judge so found; he said:
“It was clear that the phenomenon of Western separatism and the rise of the
W.C.C. were matters of public interest.” To this should be added that whatever
the plaintiff as leader of his separatist party and his followers said or did
in the public political arena in the pursuit of their controversial objective
and whatever was reported of them in the media were matters of public interest.

[
43
]

That the comment was recognized as comment by
the learned trial judge is evident from the fact that he went on to consider
the defence of fair comment.

[
44
]

It was for the plaintiff to prove malice. He did
not attempt to do so. The evidence of the plaintiff negates it.

[
45
]

In considering condition (b), that the comment
be based on fact, some authorities suggest that the fact upon which the comment
was based must be stated in the article itself. Here it is clear that it is
not, because there is no fact recited elsewhere in the article upon which to
base a comparison of the ideologies of western separatists and the Ku Klux
Klan.

[
46
]

This very issue was considered by the House of
Lords in the case of
Kemsley
v. Foot
[1952] A.C. 345
and it was
there held that the rule is not absolute when the subject matter is one that
has already been submitted to the public. Lord Porter states the issue at p.
354
et seq.:

“The question for your Lordships decision
is, therefore, whether a plea of fair comment is only permissible where the
comment is accompanied by a statement of facts upon which the comment is made
and to determine the particularity with which the facts roust be stated.”

He then says at p. 355:

“If an author writes a play or a book or a composer composes a
musical work, he is submitting that work to the public and thereby inviting
comment. Not all the public will see or read or hear it but the work is public
in the same sense as a case in the Law Courts is said to be heard in public. In
many cases it is not possible for everyone who is interested, to attend a
trial, but in so far as there is room for them in the court all are entitled to
do so, and the subject-matter upon which comment can be made is indicated to
the world at large.

The same observation is true of a newspaper. Whether the criticism
is confined to a particular issue or deals with the way in which it is in
general conducted, the subject-matter upon which criticism is made has been
submitted to the public, though by no means all those to whom the alleged libel
has been published will have seen or are likely to see the various issues.
Accordingly, its contents and conduct are open to comment on the ground that
the public have at least the opportunity of ascertaining for themselves the
subject-matter upon which the comment is founded. I am assuming that the
reference is to a known journal: for the present purpose it is not necessary to
consider how far criticism without facts upon which to base it is subject to
the same observation in the case of an obscure publication.”

.
. . .

“But the question whether an inference is a bare inference in this
sense must depend upon all the circumstances.
Indeed, it was ultimately
admitted on behalf of the appellant that the facts necessary to justify comment
might be implied from the terms of the impugned article
and therefore the
inquiry ceases to be - Can the defendant point to definite assertions of fact
in the alleged libel upon which the comment is made? and becomes - Is there
subject-matter indicated with sufficient clarity to justify comment being made?
and was the comment actually made such as an honest, though prejudiced, man
might make?”

(emphasis mine)

In the present case, the impugned words are in
obvious reference to the previously published and highly controversial
political views of the plaintiff submitted by him to the public, which the
writer considered tinged with an element of racism. These views were either
already well-known by those reading the comment, or could be readily
ascertained by them. They are implied facts upon which the comment was made.

[
47
]

The question then becomes: were any of those
published views capable of supporting the writer’s opinion of a racist similarity
between the western separatist movement and the Ku Klux Klan to justify the use
of that metaphor?

[
48
]

The thrust of the article is a criticism of the
media for giving the Western separatist movement more publicity than warranted
by its general popular support. The existence of this separatist movement is
well cataloged in the reasons for judgment of the learned trial judge, as is
the part played in it by the plaintiff and his party, the W.C.C. The learned
trial judge said. “Through this time the Plaintiff was generally seen as the
spokesperson for the H.C.C. and was intimately identified with the concept of
Western Separation.” That the separatist movement received a great deal of
publicity is a historical fact documented in the exhibits and the evidence.

[
49
]

The origin and history of the Ku Klux Klan is
recorded in history books, and resort need not be limited to expert witnesses
to take account of it. A concise history and description of its origin,
objectives and activities in the United States will be found in the Encyclopedia
Britannica, and the history of its spread and activities in Canada will be
found in the Canadian Encyclopedia (Hurtig, 1985). It stands out for its
opposition to groups not because of what these think or say or do but for what
they are by race or belief. It arose out of the American civil war in the
Southern States to intimidate blacks and northern carpetbaggers. Later it
turned against Roman Catholics and Jews. In Canada it changed its hues to
attack whatever group was perceived a threat to the supremacy of White
Anglo-Saxon Protestants. In the West it flourished mainly in Saskatchewan where
according to the evidence of Dr. Pratt, it was anti-immigration, anti-French
Canadian, anti-Catholic.

[
50
]

The two well publicized main components of the
Western separatist movement at the time when the impugned article was published
were the West-Fed organization under the helm of Elmer Knutson and the W.C.C.
led by the plaintiff, the first advocating independence by unilateral
declaration, the second through the electoral process. Many members of one were
members of the other; by October, 1981, eighty percent of the members of W.C.C.
were also members of West-Fed. Birds of a feather flock together!

[
51
]

The anti-French Canadian, anti-immigration,
anti-Quebec, anti-bilingualism, stance of the West-Fed group and its leader is
well documented in the exhibits, including its own published literature, and in
the press reports and the evidence of those who attended a large and rowdy
meeting of that group in February, 1981, where a person of East Indian origin
was made the subject of open racial slurs. This evidence could easily lead one
to honestly believe that the West-Fed group was racist.

[
52
]

The literature of the W.C.C. was not as
blatantly racist. It too opposed bilingualism and immigration. This alone could
support the conclusion that it and its leader, the plaintiff, were not far from
the West-Fed stance. A likewise large and rowdy meeting of the W.C.C. was held
in Edmonton in November, 1980, before the West-Fed rowdy meeting already
described. Of that meeting we have the evidence of Dr. Pratt who attended, and
an account appearing in the Edmonton Journal. The plaintiff was the main
speaker. Dr. Pratt described the mood of the crowd as ugly. The plaintiff
attacked French power in Ottawa, and bemoaned the fact that Quebec had not
voted for separation because this would have resolved the bilingualism issue.
According to the report of the meeting published in the Edmonton Journal.
Christie was opposed to immigrants, not on economic grounds, but because they
were prospects for Liberal votes. The report also contains the following
telling comment: “But he later told reporters: ‘Don’t call me a racist. I once
saved a French-Canadian’”, a reference to his days as a lifeguard in Banff
National Park. This might sound to some like a variant of the well known tongue
in cheek denial of his anti-semitism by the avowed anti-semitic: “Some of my
best friends are Jews.” If the plaintiff had not made comments capable of being
construed as racist remarks, why would he be concerned that reporters might
place that interpretation on them? He acknowledged and explained his remark in
cross-examination:

“A     Yes, I recall those words.

Q      Okay.

A      Because those accusations were being raised by the reporter
and that was in an interview before the meeting in the green room beside the
main stage of the Jubilee Auditorium.

Q      Did you actually save somebody who was drowning?

A      Yes.

Q      Did you know they were French-Canadian while they were in the
process of drowning?

A      No. I was trying to demonstrate that I don’t regard what is
right or wrong on the basis of anybody’s race.”

[
53
]

This facetious answer to a serious accusation
was a telling admission that at least one other reporter accused him of being a
racist.

[
54
]

These were undisputed facts disclosed in
evidence which could lead the fair-minded man described by Lord Diplock to the
view that the plaintiff was racist. Any one of those facts sufficient to
support the statement would entitle the defendants to succeed in a plea of fair
comment. In
Kerns ley, supra,
Lord Porter states at p.358:

“In the present case, for instance, the substratum of fact upon
which comment is based is that Lord Kemsley is the active proprietor of and
responsible for the Kemsley Press. The criticism is that that press is a low
one. As I hold, any facts sufficient to justify that statement would entitle
the defendants to succeed in a plea of fair comment. Twenty facts might be
given in the particulars and only one justified, yet if that one fact were
sufficient to support the comment so as to make it fair, a failure to prove the
other nineteen would not of necessity defeat the defendants’ plea.”

[
55
]

The remaining condition to be examined is
whether the defendants honestly held the views expressed.

[
56
]

This condition has been described by Lord
Denning (quoted by Ritchie J. in
Cherneskey
) as the “cardinal test” of
the defence of fair comment. The defendant testified that he honestly held the
opinions expressed and that these were not motivated by malice or ill feeling
towards the plaintiff. His evidence in this respect was not challenged in
cross-examination, and no evidence was called to contradict it. The corporate
defendant endorsed those opinions. The learned trial judge did not reject this
evidence. He said of the defendant Geiger. “My impression of this young man is
that he was an over enthusiastic young student. He was completely
anti-separatist.” Both defendants have accordingly satisfied the burden of
showing that the comments published were honestly held by them.

[
57
]

While the plaintiff may not have been racist, as
the trial judge found on his evidence, he gave to this “over enthusiastic and
completely anti-separatist young student” the honest impression that he was by
flirting with racism on the public stage on a highly charged political issue.
Lord Diplock’s test for the defence of fair comment had thus been satisfied.
Any jury properly instructed was bound to find on the evidence that the defence
of fair comment had been established.

[
58
]

I would dismiss this action with costs here and
below to be taxed on the appropriate column.

DATED at EDMONTON, Alberta

this 28th Day of October,

A.D. 1986.
